Only compare the sum with targetSum when you reach a leaf, not at an internal node.

title: Path Sum Problem

notes: A root-to-leaf path must end at a node with no children.
Negative node values mean a path sum cannot be inferred from depth or magnitude alone; every node on the selected root-to-leaf path contributes to the sum.
constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [0, 5000].
content.inputFormat: Single line: JSON array of all arguments, e.g. [arg1, arg2, ...]

sampleTestCases.explanation: The root-to-leaf paths have sums 3 and 4, so no path has sum 5.
An empty tree has no root-to-leaf path.

content.problemStatement:
With the `root` of a binary tree and an integer `targetSum`, output `true` if the tree has a **root-to-leaf** path such that adding up all the values along the path equals `targetSum`.

A **leaf** is a node with no children.

**Example 1:**

![](https://assets.leetcode.com/uploads/2021/01/18/pathsum1.jpg)

```
Input: root = [5,4,8,11,null,13,4,7,2,null,null,null,1], targetSum = 22
Output: true
Explanation: The root-to-leaf path with the target sum is shown.
```

**Example 2:**

![](https://assets.leetcode.com/uploads/2021/01/18/pathsum2.jpg)

```
Input: root = [1,2,3], targetSum = 5
Output: false
Explanation: There are two root-to-leaf paths in the tree:
(1 --> 2): The sum is 3.
(1 --> 3): The sum is 4.
There is no root-to-leaf path with sum = 5.
```

**Example 3:**

```
Input: root = [], targetSum = 0
Output: false
Explanation: Since the tree is empty, there are no root-to-leaf paths.
```

**Constraints:**

* The number of nodes in the tree is in the range `[0, 5000]`.
* `-1000 <= Node.val <= 1000`
* `-1000 <= targetSum <= 1000`

notes: Tree inputs use level-order serialization with null for missing children.
Implementations may use recursive or iterative traversal; the maximum node count is 5000.
A node contributes to a valid path only when it is on a root-to-leaf route.
The iterative stack stores at most one pending branch per tree level, so auxiliary space is O(h), where h is the tree height.
solution.approach: Traverse the binary tree from the root while carrying the sum accumulated along the current path. When a leaf is reached, return true only if the accumulated sum equals targetSum. An iterative depth-first search avoids recursion-depth issues on a 5000-node skewed tree.

better.description: Use iterative breadth-first search with a second queue of accumulated sums. This also visits each node once and avoids recursive call-stack limits, but it may store an entire tree level, requiring O(w) space where w is the maximum width.

optimal.description: Use iterative depth-first search with pairs of (node, accumulatedSum). At each node, if it is a leaf, compare its accumulated sum with targetSum. Otherwise push its children with their updated sums. This directly matches the root-to-leaf definition and uses height-bounded auxiliary storage.

bruteForce.complexity: Time O(n), auxiliary space O(h) for traversal/path state.
bruteForce.description: Enumerate every root-to-leaf path and compute its sum. A depth-first traversal visits each node and carries the current path sum, so the algorithm is already linear; an explicit path copy is unnecessary.

followUps: Can you solve the problem using breadth-first search while tracking the path sum?
How would you return the actual root-to-leaf path instead of only a boolean?
How would the implementation change if the tree could contain more than 5000 nodes?

learningObjectives: Understand root-to-leaf traversal in binary trees.
Maintain an accumulated value while traversing a tree.
Distinguish leaf nodes from internal nodes when checking a path condition.
Compare DFS and BFS auxiliary-space trade-offs.
